newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end mixed as Fed leaves rates steady.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end mixed as Fed leaves rates steady.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended a lackluster session narrowly mixed on Tuesday, after the Federal Reserve left rates steady, as expected.
"It was a long, quiet day," said Dave Connors, manager of U.S. government bond trading at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "The bond market got what it expected from the Fed: no change."
Treasuries stuck to very narrow ranges and barely moved after the Fed announced no interest rate changes. Whatever price movement there was took place at the long end.
The 30-year bond closed at 98-6/32, up 3/32 from late Monday. Its yield dipped to 6.51 percent from 6.52 percent.
Meanwhile, the two-year note fell 1/32 to 100-3/32, with its yield rising to 5.84 percent from 5.80 percent.
As such, the spread between the two-year and 30-year narrowed to 67 basis points from 72 basis points on Monday.
"It seems like there was a lot of curve trading today," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
Throughout the day, players reported the unwidning of steepening trades made during Friday's big stock market fall.
Money from stocks flowed into the short end of the bond market Friday, when the Dow Jones industrial average dove three percent, resulting in a steepening of the yield curve.

Traders also said numerous accounts put on curve flattening trades Tuesday, in the hopes the curve would narrow further ahead of next week's two- and five-year note auctions. And, some retail players moved from two-year notes into five-year notes.
But activity was rather thin. According to GovPx, volume was about $70 billion, with much of the action in the early morning.

Treasuries opened weaker, as the settlement between United Parcel Service and its striking Teamsters union was viewed as a negative during overseas trading during the night. Traders feared the wage gains scored by the Teamsters union may spill over to others, potentially sparking inflation.
The market edged higher after the Bundesbank left its repo rate alone.
As for the U.S. day, "it was quite uneventful," Dimick said.
The market brushed aside an unchanged housing starts number for July and a 0.7 percent rise in the Redbook Research weekly retail sales report.

And the Fed meeting was similarly a non-event, since there was a zero chance of a rate hike priced in. One trader said that the lack of the usual "relief rally" was due to widespread expectation of the Fed keeping rates steady.
"You have to have at least a 10 percent chance of a rate hike priced in," he said.
The more important item, players said, will be the release of the minutes on Friday of the prior Fed policy meeting from early July.
The market does not anticpate a rate hike until November at the earliest.
Treasuries were expected to remain locked in tight ranges for the foreseeable future, with the 30-year bond seen having trouble breaching below the 6.50 percent level.
On Wednesday, June trade data are due, but players said the bond market won't react unless the dollar does.
In late trading, three-month bills were down one basis point at 5.09 percent. Six-month bills were down one basis point at 5.14 percent and year bills were up one basis point at 5.22 percent.

The 10-year issue was unchanged at 99-12/32 to yield 6.21 percent. The five-year note was 1/32 lower at 99-24/32 to yield 6.06 percent and the three-year note was down 2/32 at 100-3/32 to yield 5.97 percent.
